name: The Hole Under the Mountain
summary: There is one mouth in the east massif, everybody knows where it is, and the ground around it forgets on a clock you can time with a candle.
body: Everything else in this book is the world working as it always has. This chapter is not that.

There is a cave under the eastern mountain. It has one mouth, it is not hidden, and every single person in Nangijala can tell you roughly where it is. There is no legend about finding it. The whole difficulty has always been the other direction.

That is the plain observation, and it was made carefully, by people who did not want it to be true. Ground that had been held for centuries — good ground, in the rota, with a fire on it — went soft in a season. Then the season became a month. A keeper working the eastern circuit reported that she had lost the name of her own fire while walking toward the mouth and had it back within an hour of walking away, and she was not a woman anybody had ever known to lose anything.
Things that go in come out wrong, or come out wearing something else's face, or do not come out.

The creatures around it are not like the creatures anywhere else, and anybody who has been near both can tell the difference immediately. Out in the world a beast is a shape that outlasted its occupant — it is running on habit, it is empty, and there is something almost restful about how uninterested it is in you. The things near the mouth are not empty in that way. They were emptied. It happened to them, all at once, and something is still wearing the outside.

When you break one, a mask comes down out of it and lands in the dirt, and it is still smiling. This is the detail that started the entire investigation, because the mask does not thin. Nothing about it goes soft. It sits there afterwards being exactly a face, indefinitely, long after everything else about the creature has stopped being anywhere at all.
There is a great deal of argument about what is down there and none of it is worth writing down yet. Two things, though, are worth stating, because both are checkable and both are unsettling.

The first is that the hole is new. Not new the way a season is new — new the way a wound is. The Age of Fires had no hole under the eastern mountain. There are people still walking around, thinning quietly, who remember when the east road was simply a road, and if you buy them an evening they will tell you what the ground there used to feel like.

The second is that whatever is down there is not angry with anybody. Nothing about it is angry. It has never once been observed to do anything out of malice, or vengeance, or any of the ordinary reasons a thing does harm.
It is hungry. That is all it is. The tellers say that is worse, and the tellers are right.
